settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: The fallback is an intentional, documented behavior (comment says 'to allow custom unknown protocols')
The check requires the lowercased value to start with 'protocol:' for one of the configured protocols, which bounds what can pass
isValidAnchor additionally rejects anchor values containing whitespace
Default whitelists (basic/relaxed) restrict protocols to a fixed allowlist; no test in the repo demonstrates an actual bypass
candidates.description: Whitelist.testValidProtocol resolves the attribute value to an absolute URL via el.absUrl(attr.getKey()); if that yields an empty string it falls back to the raw attribute value ('if it could not be made abs, run as-is to allow custom unknown protocols'). It then accepts the value if, for any allowed protocol, value.toLowerCase().startsWith(protocol + ":"). This is a prefix match rather than full URI parsing, so a value that merely begins with an allowed protocol token (e.g. containing additional characters/whitespace or control characters after the scheme) is accepted as long as it starts with the allowed token. When preserveRelativeLinks is false, the (possibly raw) value is written back to the attribute. A caller using the whitelist for strict URL-attribute validation could therefore pass through values not strictly conforming to an allowed protocol.
missing_evidence: No dynamic test or CVE reference in the repo demonstrating a concrete bypass payload
Unknown whether a caller in a real deployment passes untrusted, unresolvable URIs with misleading prefixes
No confirmation of how el.absUrl handles unusual schemes/whitespace in this version
preconditions: Caller uses Cleaner/Whitelist with addProtocols and relies on it for strict URL attribute validation
Untrusted HTML supplies a URL attribute (e.g. a[href], img[src]) whose value begins with an allowed protocol token but is not a canonical absolute URL
Attribute value cannot be resolved against the document base URI (or base URI absent), triggering the raw-value fallback
candidates.title: URL attribute whitelist uses prefix matching with raw fallback (potential sanitizer bypass)

counter_evidence: Validation is enabled by default (validateTSLCertificates = true)
The method is an explicit opt-in API and its Javadoc documents the insecure trust manager and verifier
Behavior only applies when the caller disables validation
candidates.description: HttpConnection.Request defaults validateTSLCertificates to true (line 360). However, when validateTLSCertificates(false) is called, Response.createConnection installs an all-trusting X509TrustManager (checkClientTrusted/checkServerTrusted are no-ops, getAcceptedIssuers returns null) and a HostnameVerifier that always returns true, via initUnSecureTSL. This disables both certificate-chain and hostname validation for subsequent HTTPS connections, exposing them to man-in-the-middle attacks. This is an explicitly exposed API (Connection.validateTLSCertificates).
missing_evidence: No evidence that any application code in scope calls validateTLSCertificates(false)
No evidence of untrusted influence over that setting
preconditions: Caller explicitly invokes validateTLSCertificates(false) on the request/connection
The connection targets an https URL
candidates.title: TLS certificate and hostname validation can be disabled, installing an all-trusting trust manager

counter_evidence: Validate only checks non-empty name / non-null value, not content
Reachability depends entirely on the caller providing untrusted header/cookie data
Underlying HttpURLConnection may reject some malformed values on certain JDKs
candidates.description: getRequestCookieString concatenates cookie names and values directly into a single Cookie header with no escaping/validation (the code comment itself notes no escaping is defined). Request headers supplied via header(name, value) are also added verbatim via conn.addRequestProperty. If a caller passes untrusted data into header/cookie names or values, characters such as CR/LF can be injected into the outgoing HTTP request, enabling header/request splitting or cookie smuggling. Note that processResponseHeaders extracts Set-Cookie values from server responses and stores them as cookies, which are then echoed back on subsequent/redirect requests.
missing_evidence: No in-repo demonstration that untrusted data reaches these setters
No test showing actual CRLF injection through addRequestProperty
preconditions: Caller passes untrusted input into header(name,value) or cookie(name,value)/cookies(map)
Resulting request is executed against a server influenced by the attacker
candidates.title: Unescaped header/cookie values allow request header injection

counter_evidence: fromJsoup/convert build the W3C DOM programmatically rather than parsing XML, so no external entities are resolved in this code path
No parsing of untrusted XML occurs within W3CDom itself
candidates.description: W3CDom instantiates DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance() with default settings (protected field, line 29) and a TransformerFactory.newInstance() for serialization, without explicitly disabling DTD/external entity features or setting secure-processing attributes. The W3C document here is produced programmatically from a jsoup document (createElement/createTextNode/createComment), so no untrusted XML is parsed by this path, which limits direct XXE exposure. The observation is that the factory is left at platform defaults, so any future use that parses XML with this factory could be exposed depending on the JDK defaults.
missing_evidence: No caller in scope shown to parse untrusted XML with this factory
No evidence of actual XXE reachability
preconditions: A subclass or caller reuses the exposed 'factory' field to parse untrusted XML input
The platform JDK defaults leave external entities enabled
candidates.title: Default XML factory configuration without explicit external-entity hardening in W3CDom
